Suppression du ministère de la Diversité: The Ministry of Diversity, Inclusion and Persons with Disabilities has been eliminated. A “symbolic recognition that is collapsing.”

Le nouveau conseil des ministres du gouv: The new federal cabinet boasts exemplary gender parity and good representation of diversity. Yet despite this appearance of inclusivity, the Ministry of Diversity, Inclusion and Persons with Disabilities has been removed from the federal cabinet, only six years after it was created.
La décision soulève de nombreuses questi: The decision raises many questions among citizens, researchers, community organizations and activists. It is all the more surprising because it comes from the former Liberal government, now led by Mark Carney. “We voted Liberal thinking this ministry would last,” says one of the people we met. The sense of disappointment is widely shared within this community.
Dans ce premier article, je m’intéresse: In this first article, I look at the repercussions of this disappearance, particularly for people with disabilities, many of whom are also from diverse backgrounds and find themselves at the intersection of several forms of marginalization. Experts and organizations also voice their concerns, especially in Quebec, where budget cuts have grown since 2024.
‍<strong><em>Depuis la fin de 2024, les: ‍Since the end of 2024, services for people with disabilities have suffered several budget cuts in Quebec. Adapted transportation, accessible housing, home care: the setbacks are many. But it is a federal decision that has caused the greatest shock: the disappearance, without any official announcement, of the Ministry of Diversity, Inclusion and Persons with Disabilities, barely six years after its creation in 2019. For the 23% of Canadians who live with a disability, this elimination goes beyond a simple administrative reorganization. “It’s a symbolic recognition that is collapsing,” sums up Lila H. Ratsifa, executive director of the Association multiethnique pour l’intégration des personnes handicapées (AMEIPH). What place is concretely given to these citizens? And above all, what will be the consequences of such a decision on their daily lives, which are already full of obstacles? We went to meet people who live this reality day in and day out. Our report.
<strong>Montréal, le mercredi 21 mai.</s: Montréal, Wednesday, May 21. One week after the new cabinet was unveiled, on Saint-Laurent Street, a red door opens onto an unassuming building. Inside, on the top floor, we meet Lila Ratsifa, accompanied by Martha Twibanire, an active member of the association. With a frank smile, Martha wears a bright blue jacket and ginger hair styled in an afro. Polio took the use of her legs when she was 10 years old. In 1999, she fled Rwanda after losing her husband and one of her children in the genocide. Today she lives in Montréal, uses a wheelchair and works as a bank advisor.
« Je viens d’apprendre que le ministère: “I just found out that the ministry that represented us is gone. What does that mean? That we’re too much? That we’re a nuisance?” She pauses, then adds: “I pay my taxes. I contribute. As a bank advisor, I’ve helped dozens of people become homeowners. And yet, they’re trying to make me disappear. As if I didn’t count.”
Pour elle, la disparition du ministère d: For her, the disappearance of the Ministry of Diversity, Inclusion and Persons with Disabilities is a worrying signal: “They see us as a burden, not as full citizens. They don’t see our value,” she lets out.
Lila le confirme. « On a regardé la comp: Lila confirms it. “We looked at the makeup of the new cabinet. We’re happy to see gender parity, to see racialized people… that’s good. But not a single person has a disability.”
« On espère que la suppression de ce min: “We hope the elimination of this ministry is solely because they understood how much disability cuts across several ministries: health, housing, transportation, immigration… But we’re also afraid that if no one defends a global vision, it will get diluted. And what gets diluted gets lost.”
Dans l’entrée, Emmanuel Mupesse apparaît: In the entryway, Emmanuel Mupesse appears. Blue coat, dark glasses, navy cap. At 72, this retiree of Congolese origin lives with a visual impairment. He sits down slowly and speaks in a measured way: “Me too, I worked my whole life. I came with my diplomas, my licence, my papers. I followed the rules. Canada welcomed me, yes, but that means it has to accommodate me too. Even if I’m disabled.”
Il soupire. « Je me suis dit : votons li: He sighs. “I told myself: let’s vote Liberal, things will get better. But now, I’m lost.”
« Peut-être que Mark Carney ne connaît t: “Maybe Mark Carney just doesn’t know anyone with a disability,” Martha quips with a slight laugh.
« Depuis mon arrivée au Canada, il y a 2: “Since I arrived in Canada 25 years ago, there has been progress, it’s true,” she continues, more seriously. “Adapted transportation, for example. But those are things we had to wrest away. Nothing was offered to us. Every little bit of progress, you have to fight for it. And often, you have to fight again so you don’t lose it.”
La disparition du ministère est interpré: The ministry’s disappearance is seen as a repudiation. Even though the management of services for people with disabilities falls largely under provincial jurisdiction, this federal decision carries a very heavy symbolic weight. “We feel erased. As if we were good for nothing,” Emmanuel murmurs.
Les récits des problèmes auxquels ils so: Accounts of the problems they already face every day follow one after another: scornful looks, housing refusals, inaccessible public spaces and homes. “There are young disabled adults who are placed in seniors’ residences for lack of adapted housing!” Martha exclaims, frowning. “At 24, you should be having friends over, listening to music, living your youth. Not ending up living with an 85-year-old…”
<strong>« Beaucoup de personnes ont voté: “Many people voted for the Liberals thinking this ministry would stay, but in the end, it’s gone”
Maude Massicotte, cofondatrice de DéfPhy: Maude Massicotte, cofounder of DéfPhys Sans Limite, an organization that defends the rights of young adults with disabilities aged 18 to 30, shares the same view. She appears on screen. Hair down and a discreet smile. Maude is 33 and lives with a disability herself, facial paralysis, and uses a wheelchair.
« Je suis allée à Québec le 14 mai pour: “I went to Quebec City on May 14 to protest,” she begins. “It was the consultation day, with the ministers of Health and Seniors, on the new home care services plan. But they talked exclusively about older people. Nothing about people with disabilities. It feels like, to get a minimum of services, you have to get old…”
Elle poursuit : « Il y a des personnes e: She continues: “There are people with disabilities who are only entitled to one or two baths a week. Otherwise, it’s a washcloth. And if you live with your boyfriend or a family member? They cut your help with housework, with meal preparation... You become dependent on the person who lives with you.”
Mais le coup le plus dur, pour elle, est: But the hardest blow, for her, is the elimination of the federal ministry responsible for people with disabilities.
« C’est comme si on disparaissait une de: “It’s like we’re disappearing a second time,” she continues. “We’re already barely seen. Now they’re outright removing the only political space that was dedicated to us.” In the same breath, she goes on: “We’re angry! When Trudeau left, the ministry disappeared. We wanted to believe it was temporary. We hoped that with the formation of the new cabinet, we’d get that representation back. But no. Nothing. Many people voted for the Liberals thinking this ministry would stay, but in the end, it’s gone.”
Le sentiment d’être invisible est pesant: The feeling of being invisible weighs heavily, Maude shares. And according to her, when no one with a disability sits at the table, policies don’t reflect the full reality of Canadian citizens.
<strong>« Ça prend une personne en situa: “It takes a person with a disability in government to understand our reality”
Elle se souvient de l'influence qu’avait: She remembers the influence of the previous minister, Carla Qualtrough, who herself has a disability and who championed the Canada Disability Benefit, a monthly payment of $200 for people living below the poverty line.
« On dirait que ça prend une personne en: “It seems like it takes a person with a disability in government to understand our reality,” she says, raising her hands. “She knew what she was talking about. She fought for this benefit. But now there’s no ministry and no minister with a disability; so we wonder: if there’s no one like us in cabinet, who’s going to fight in our place?”
Maude exprime une crainte partagée par l: Maude expresses a fear shared by the members of her organization: that the ministry’s disappearance will lead to further setbacks and that the few hard-won gains are now on borrowed time.
« Au Québec, ils ont déjà commencé à cou: “In Quebec, they’ve already started cutting home adaptation. We’re talking about thousands of dollars that people now have to pay out of their own pockets to make their homes accessible.”
Elle conclut d’un ton sec : « On nous do: She concludes in a curt tone: “They give us $200, but they cut everywhere else. It’s an illusion of a social safety net.”
<strong>Des intérêts économiques au détr: Economic interests at the expense of people with disabilities?
Pour Normand Boucher, sociologue et poli: For Normand Boucher, a sociologist and political scientist who specializes in disability policy, the elimination of the ministry reveals the country’s new interests in the context of the trade war with the United States. “The priority is the economy, then giving Canadians a new identity,” he explains, alluding to the new Ministry of Canadian Identity and Society.
Ce recentrage économique se reflète dans: This economic refocusing is reflected in the very language of decision-makers, he adds. “When disability is discussed, it’s always from a cost perspective. Disability is seen as a problem for the economy, as a burden.” For him, this view is dangerous, because it reduces citizens to their potential economic productivity, further marginalizing those who don’t fit that mould.
L’expert souligne en outre que cette log: The expert also points out that this logic of reshuffling is driven by a renewed government team, but one oriented toward technocratic governance. “The current prime minister clearly wanted to set himself apart from his predecessor. He appointed about ten new ministers who weren’t there under Trudeau. These are people who haven’t necessarily been driven by political struggles, but by a more managerial vision of the state.”
Résultat ? Les enjeux sociaux passent à: The result? Social issues move to the background, especially those affecting people with disabilities. “This ministry was a symbol. Its disappearance sends a message: these are no longer front-line issues.”
Mais pour le sociologue, ce n’est pas qu: But for the sociologist, this is not just a symbolic matter; it is a very concrete step backward, particularly because Canadian governance rests on a complex division of responsibilities between the federal government and the provinces. “The federal government doesn’t deliver services. It transfers funds to the provinces, which use them as they see fit. The result: territorial inequalities are enormous. Living in Vancouver or in Winnipeg is not at all the same experience when you use a wheelchair.”
« Au Québec, un fauteuil roulant, c’est: “In Quebec, a wheelchair is a collective good,” he continues. “It’s funded by taxes. In Ontario, 50% is paid by the individual. That’s far from an equitable model.”
Et ce recul s’accompagne d’un retour à l: And this setback comes with a return to a charity-based logic: “There’s more and more reliance on charity, on private foundations. Disability is a collective responsibility. Now we’re going back to the idea that it’s up to the individual to manage their disability with their own means.”
Or, pour l’expert, cette fragilité des d: For the expert, this fragility of the rights of people with disabilities carries heavy consequences. “It reminds us that nothing is ever permanently secured, and that applies to all marginalized groups. There’s this feeling of fragility. Rights are never guaranteed. The context can change very quickly. What we’re seeing in the United States or in Europe proves it, moreover.”
Contacté par La Converse, le cabinet du: Contacted by La Converse, the prime minister’s office replied that “the work to support Canadians living with disabilities and to promote diversity continues within the relevant departments, both within government and on the political side.” While the Ministry of Diversity, Inclusion and Persons with Disabilities has been dissolved, two ministers now take on these responsibilities.
Patty Hajdu, ministre de l’Emploi et des: Patty Hajdu, Minister of Jobs and Families, will be responsible for disability files, notably the reform of the Disability Tax Credit and the development of a justice framework for people with disabilities. For his part, Minister Steven Guilbeault will take charge of diversity initiatives, including making permanent the funding of the 2SLGBTQI+ Community Capacity Fund.
Aucune explication n’a toutefois été don: However, no explanation has been given for the formal elimination of the ministry or the lack of a public announcement about it.
Lila H. Ratsifa, directrice générale de: Lila H. Ratsifa, executive director of AMEIPH, assures us that the organization and its partners are getting organized to prepare a statement that will be sent to the government. Their wish is for every ministry to include a service dedicated to people with disabilities. “It’s also our role, as an organization, to proclaim loud and clear the importance of having these structures responsible for people with disabilities in the various ministries,” she concludes.
